pr_title: promtool: backfill: allow configuring block duration
pr_body:
When backfilling large amounts of data across long periods of time, it
may in certain circumstances be useful to use a longer block duration to
increase the efficiency and speed of the backfilling process. This patch
adds a flag --block-duration-power to allow a user to choose the power N
where the block duration is 2^(N+1)h.

Signed-off-by: Steve Kuznetsov <skuznets@redhat.com>

---
Fixes https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/8388
Builds on top of #8917 so as to not create merge conflicts. I do not know the best place to leave the discussion about block durations, so I added it to the helptext. I certainly think it is useful for users who are not familiar with TSDB basics to have that discussion present when they are choosing a block duration.
/assign @roidelapluie @brian-brazil
pr_comments:
Thanks.

I prefer to have the duration of the blocks, as it would be more telling for the users. Power is really obscure and it's an implementation detail.

We could in the help list a few examples (2h, 4h, 8h).

If you think it is too much to ask for the user, we could round down the duration provided (with a warning). e.g. if you pass 20h you would have 16h blocks. But I don't think it is necessary for a first step.

Note: the documentation should be on the storage page.

I disagree - in your code you very specifically validate this `2^(N+1)h` rule. Why should we expose a flag to users where the vast majority of values are wrong? In the other thread you and @brian-brazil were very clear that choosing an incorrect value of duration is very bad, and only a very narrow range of durations would ever work. Why should we allow users to choose wrong values, only to validate them and send them an error? The only real choice users have is the `N` in the above equation, so that's what they should provide IMHO.

> Note: the documentation should be on the storage page.

@roidelapluie sorry, would you mind linking where this page is, so I could edit it?
Moved the conversation about when to use the flag to `docs/storage.md`

What if, if we reject, we print to stderr the value below and above? So the user can pick easily?

I am really affraid that users will write "24" or even "10", making gigantic blocks by accident, plus this is adding a lot of complexity (you need to compute the power instead of picking from the few examples we show in the --help)

The other way to think about this is this is an API (ok, outside the Prometheus API stability guarantees currently), but by forcing this to be a particular power it means this becomes coupled to the implementation of the block storage.

By using a duration that is validated, it's nicer to users but also does not get in the way of any potential (even if unlikely) changes to the block format.

@dgl the maintainers made it very clear to me that a) only very specific values are allowed b) if you use other values, things will go very wrong. What is the benefit of planning for an unlikely future where the default block size changes? I want to build a useful tool _today_ that makes it impossible for users to make the wrong decision, in a space where the decision is hard to make and incorrect choices are deleterious.

@roidelapluie IDK if you and other maintainers feel really strongly I can change it but I honestly believe that giving users an infinite input space, making it *seem* like there's choice, and validating it down to very, very distinct values is simply terrible UX. Compare the two cases:

1. the user has a `--block-duration-power` flag, reads the documentation on how to use it, chooses a power and goes from there
2. the user has a `--block-duration` flag, makes a guess, chooses an invalid duration, has to go read the doc to figure out which values are valid, implicitly chooses a power, goes from there

Why is 2 better?

edit: and, overall - I've been lead to understand by @brian-brazil that this choice is very specific, very hard to do right and very important. I explicitly do *not* want users to have an easy time choosing any old random duration without understanding what will happen to their TSDB afterword. If this flag *doesn't* lead people to read the doc and make an informed decision after thinking through the implications, that's a failure in my book. There is no simple choice to make and  there is no simple duration they can use other than the default.

I am quite confident that we should not expose those kind of details to our users.

What we could to is to propose a --max-block-duration=2h option instead, and we take the power of 2 below it.

--max-block-duration=24h would create 16h blocks.

@roidelapluie that is a good approach as well. Do we expect users to want a specific max value, or should we add something like `--use-largest-blocks` that looks at the input OpenMetrics data and simply chooses the block size that would fit all of the data? Or maybe a `--split-across-blocks=N` and choose some "correct" duration whereby N blocks result?
--use-largest-blocks will probably be too big for e.g. 1 year of data. `--split-across-blocks=N` might work but it would also lie to the user which has data for less than e.g. 2 hours.
@roidelapluie what would be reasonable bounds for the block size? No smaller than 2h and no larger than a week? A month? three months?

@roidelapluie ok - I've added the flag to choose a number of blocks and added validation so it's not too large or too small. I chose a random value for the largest allowable block, but please take a look and advise me as to the best option here.
(I think we'll need to do the close/reopen thing here too to get CircleCI to run?)

I still don't think this is the correct fix. I stand by my proposal of a max block duration because that is what you pass to the prometheus server. Then you can have the same max block duration on backfill and prometheus. Prometheus does not have the option "keep 10 blocks".

@roidelapluie you should have said so... your previous comments definitely sounded like you endorsing this approach. With a duration, though, could you please explain to me why it's the better approach to ask the user for a raw duration when almost all possible values are invalid? Does `prometheus` do the same validation when you pass it a block duration flag?
If passed storage.tsdb.max-block-duration=24h, prometheus would create blocks up to 16h, like in my proposal. I would not error.
We ask the user for a max duration, not for an exact duration. That mimics the options of Prometheus, so it is safe for users to use the same value as their Prometheus server.
Well, ya should have said that! If it's an existing UX used elsewhere, there's nothing to do but copy it here :)

(to be fair, the code you linked me that you wrote did the validation and sent an error... I would really love to have learned of the Prometheus TSDB flag earlier so we could have saved SO much time talking about all this ...)
Code now uses identical logic to the `--storage.tsdb.max-block-duration` flag in the main `prometheus` binary.
@roidelapluie I'm not sure how you got CircleCI to work on my other PR but I think you will need to use that magic again here :|
@codesome thanks for the review! Updated

@codesome  of course - added a test for a longer duration. Let me know if it's ok, but I also changed the tests to run using Go subtests so I could iterate more quickly on one test case, and added failure messages to the asserts as they were pretty cryptic before. There was one assert I simply removed because to my eyes all it did was ensure that all blocks were the default duration long - without a message I can't be sure.

> There was one assert I simply removed because to my eyes all it did was ensure that all blocks were the default duration long

Let's bring that back. We need to ensure that the blocks don't cross the expected size and also the boundaries defined by those block duration. `testBlocks` can take an additional argument for expected block duration, and the test case struct can include that info (since max is not always the block duration). To keep it simple, 0 in the struct could mean the default block duration.
@codesome sure - added tests for those edges and wrote a check for the span of all blocks.
@codesome thanks for the thorough review! Hopefully the English wording in the tests makes it easier what, specifically, is being asserted about for the next bloke to break them ;)
Closed and reopened to re-run the CI as they were stuck
CI is failing, looks like you are missing gofmt on your changes :)
@codesome haha sorry! Fighting with a new editor setup :facepalm:

issue_context.title: Backfill: change default block size
issue_context.body:
With the newly introduced backfill command, we are creating 2-hour blocks. For a year it is more than 4000 blocks.

It would be nice if we could either automatically compact them or change the default duration of the blocks (there is a TODO for this in code).

Either via a --block-duration flag or --enable-compations and prometheus compaction flags (max block size etc).
comments: +1 for `--block-duration` since a bigger block duration can make backfill faster (since we iterate through the input file for every block). Compactions can be left to Prometheus to take care of and not required to have it in 2 places.
Any duration which is not a factor of 2h could cause problems when it comes to compaction later on.

Do we have a guarantee about alignment in TSDB?

What happens with block size = 8h and a situation like this, is it possible?

![blocksize](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/291750/105841420-d5d2ce80-5fd4-11eb-9d1f-cfa224da8f2a.png)


Do all the prometheus TSDB's use the same "boundaries" ?
That's not possible with Prometheus currently, and I believe would end poorly with the current code.

@roidelapluie @brian-brazil howdy! I'd love to work on this, but I lack the subject matter expertise to understand this fully. Some questions I'd love some input on:

- is it a hard requirement that block durations are a multiple of two hours?
- if so, would it be more appropriate to expose `--block-duration-multiplier` or something and apply that to the base 2h size?
- what is the result of the conversation above w.r.t. alignment in TSDB? I can't parse the conclusion
- as a user without deep knowledge of TSDB internals, what are my actual needs? Why would I ever *not* choose a block size as large as required to contain all of my data that I'm backfilling? What are the tradeoffs between larger and smaller sizes? How would I go about choosing the correct one?
I have done this for the graphite exporter: https://github.com/prometheus/graphite_exporter/pull/145

Mostly though I think from a user perspective where I am not a Prometheus/TSDB expert, I'm not really sure that I want to tell the tool anything about the block duration. I mostly want to make my backfill fast :)

So, to that end - how would I choose a duration? Why would I ever choose a duration that's shorter than the smallest duration that fully covers my input dataset? What are the drawbacks to this?

> is it a hard requirement that block durations are a multiple of two hours?

No, but things will almost certainly go wrong unless you know exactly what you're doing.

> if so, would it be more appropriate to expose --block-duration-multiplier or something and apply that to the base 2h size?

Maybe, however a non-trivial number of users have ignored instruction to not mess around with block sizes and compaction settings (e.g. the majority of Thanos users) so this may also cause problems with them. And you still need to worry about alignment.

> Why would I ever not choose a block size as large as required to contain all of my data that I'm backfilling?

After compaction it can cause one block covering all of that time period, plus every other block overlapping it. Such a mega block is not desirable.

> As I understand it, you're saying that other projects / derivative users of TSDB like Thanos are not using the same default block size,

No, Thanos users of Prometheus have different block sizes on disk than a Prometheus with default settings would have. The alignment is generally the same for these, but they'd only ever want 2h blocks.

> Why is a mega block not desirable? 

At the simplest, time-based retention won't work as as long as one part of the potentially years-long block is in range it has to be kept. Conversely with size-based retention, data will be deleted far too soon. You can't compact with such a block, without producing more mega blocks which could leave you with lots of blocks around if you backfill regularly.

@brian-brazil thanks for all the clarifications! One last question: is it possible after connecting to a TSDB instance to figure out a) what the default block size it has been configured to use and b) how to align the blocks? I can't see any alignment happening in the backfill command right now, is that because the current code doesn't actually talk to the TSDB directly, instead simply writing data to the directory? Is this also why it's required to restart Prometheus after backfilling to get the data fully ingested?

1) It is not an information stored, but I would assume 2h. I don't think we should support something different in this tool.

2) The blocks are already aligned in the current code:
https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/d44b4c5f1da2b7e84ad86c73cfde05ca030595c1/cmd/promtool/backfill.go#L70
It should not be required to restart Prometheus with the more recent version, we should see the data within 1 minute.

> It is not an information stored, but I would assume 2h. I don't think we should support something different in this tool.

More particularly we don't know what values might have been used previously, but 2h is reasonable to presume.

Thanks all for the pointers and explanations, I appreciate you taking your time to help me understand. I've tried to expose the option to change the duration (along with a discussion of when this might be appropriate and what the drawbacks might be) in #8919 .
FWIW with the fix from #8919 and a block duration that spans my entire dataset, a 1min import now takes 500ms.

review_comments:
While this is testing the max block duration, we are missing some edge cases. Here are my suggestions for the test cases:

(Reference: `ExponentialBlockRanges(2, 10, 3) -> [2 6 18 54 162 486 1458 4374 13122 39366]`)

1. 3 samples of same series such that 2 of them fall in the same block and 1 in another block. With max block duration same as right now (2048h), is 1458h.

(t, t+1400h, t+1500h)
```
http_requests_total{code="200"} 1 1624463088.000
http_requests_total{code="200"} 2 1629503088.000
http_requests_total{code="200"} 3 1629863088.000
```

2. Same as above, but with max block duration much more than `> 39366h`. So lets keep it `200000h` (basically >3x of largest block).

(t, t+39300h, t+40000h)
```
http_requests_total{code="200"} 1 1624463088.000
http_requests_total{code="200"} 2 1765943088.000
http_requests_total{code="200"} 3 1768463088.000
```

Expected number of blocks in both cases is 2.
